description: We're thinking about either tackling PlanetX and SPHEREx or Lunar Landing Sight Navigator. We are open to anyone who wants to join us and create something interesting while having fun!
summary: SPHEREX Blink is a web tool designed to help fight objects that move or have changed in NASA's newest infrared sky survey. This tool allows you to flip between images from both the SphereX and WISE telescopes to see the differences in each year that the images were taken. This works by combining the exposures from each visit into a clean picture and line them up as a timeline that can be scrolled through. We also have a feature that highlights each change in the picture which aids in finding tiny differences in each picture! This feature is called Flux where green highlights the increase in flux and magenta where it fell. New SPHEREx data arrives weekly and this tool accommodates this by reading the images straight from NASA's Amazon S3 archive, so the latest sky view is only mere seconds away. Anyone can use this tool to explore the survey and help to look for what's moving out there!
details:
What it does and how it works

SPHEREX Blink is a web page for spotting what moves or changes in the sky. You can either enter a star name, galaxy, or coordinates which then finds every image using NASA's archive, then combines the exposures from each visit into one clean picture, then aligns every picture to the same sky grind, and finally blinks through them as a timeline and allows you to jump through each image or through a playback. The benef

Benefits and intended impact

Objects that move against the background stars are close to us. Using our tool makes the experience much easier and streamlined by allowing you to do one quick search to see any star and then to blink through each image collected by NASA telescopes.

Tools and technology

Backend: Python with FastAPI. Image processing uses NumPy, SciPy, Astropy (reading FITS image files and sky coordinates) and reproject (aligning images).

Frontend: plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no framework. Images are drawn on the HTML Canvas with an upscaling and sharpening step.

Data: NASA/IPAC IRSA search services. Images are read straight from NASA’s public Amazon S3 buckets, fetching only the bytes needed instead of whole files.

Hosting: Render, which redeploys automatically from GitHub.

Development: Git and GitHub. We used Claude Code as an AI coding assistant.

What makes it creative

Instead of a small image boxed inside a dashboard, the telescope image fills the entire screen, so you feel like you’re looking through the telescope yourself. From there you can search any star and blink through more than 15 years of infrared history, from WISE in 2010 to SPHEREx today, without ever leaving the sky.

Factors we considered

The biggest factor that we considered for this project was speed. When we first retrieved the data using IRSA the speed of the image collection was extremely slow. We decided to instead use Amazon S3 instead of the cutout service thus caching the results on the disk, loading images in parallel, and a script that pre-loads the examples before a demo. We also wanted to make sure that this tool was reliable in case of any downtime from Amazon services therefore we made it so that it default falls back to the IRSA if S3 fails and reusing saved searches when the archive is down.
